data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The primary driver of the nocturnal UHI is the delayed release of sensible heat from high thermal mass materials (asphalt, concrete), and the cross-city intensity gap scales with building height and street canyon geometry via reduced sky view factor.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If rural thermal mass (e.g., bare rock) matches urban mass, the gap collapses.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If high winds mix the boundary layer thoroughly, canyon trapping fails and the gap narrows.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Urban materials have high thermal mass and heat capacity, storing intense daytime sensible heat. After sunset, they release this stored heat slowly via longwave radiation. In denser cities, tall buildings form street canyons that trap this radiation by reducing the sky view factor, severely limiting radiative cooling to the sky. Therefore, cities with taller buildings and deeper canyons retain heat longer, making the nighttime gap larger.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
